correspondence.finding: The southern endpoint approaches northwest west of Olavarría, turns near Blanca Grande and continues northeast. The atlas resolves Brandsen and the subsequent Las Flores corridor; the national account describes Brandsen feeding Blanca Grande and Las Flores leaving it. The southernmost modeled feeder is left unnamed, and the lake passage is not renamed as a river.

The selected line runs northeast past the General Alvear setting, south of Saladillo, then east and north through the Las Flores confluence lowlands. This corresponds to the separate Las Flores approach, not the upper Salado route. The national account distinguishes the Flores Grande lake, Chileno and Canal 16 connections; these provide network context without assigning each modeled link an official channel name.

After the confluence southeast of Roque Pérez, the selection follows the Salado east/southeast through the Monte–General Belgrano setting. Its subsequent pronounced southern bend north of Castelli and turn northeast to the coast match the atlas's repeatedly labeled Río Salado. Canal 15, drawn separately farther south, is not an alias or replacement for this selected terminal route.

The selected eastern endpoint corresponds to the Salado's Bahía Samborombón outlet setting. The southern grouped feeder enters near the lower-course bend, amid the separate Camarones/Gualicho and engineered-drainage network. The sources support that regional context, without establishing one hydronym for every part of this model-linked feeder or an exact tidal shoreline vertex.

The grouped northern branch follows the upper Salado through the Junín lake district and the Bragado–Alberti/Chivilcoy corridor to the lower junction, although the model calls it tributary. The western branch occupies the Vallimanca–Saladillo lowlands, where the provincial plan distinguishes streams, wetlands and artificial drainage. These relationships support a Salado-system representative name, not a blanket rename of all nine pieces.

correspondence: The complete single selected line was inspected: the eastern southward leg, the long westward interior run, its broad southern trough, the northwestward rise and final short western sequence. No additional tributary fragment is present.

The long eastern and central sections occupy mapped Inland Ice. The western sequence approaches the western ice/land margin north/northeast of the mapped Søndre Strømfjord locality. Readable graticule, land/ice configuration and the actual sequence of bends support regional feature-class correspondence, not a named-river alignment.

The original map does not establish this entire line as one named surface river, subglacial river or glacier. No nearby locality, fjord or possible marginal-stream name is transferred to the full interior route; its exact terminal natural-feature identity remains unassigned.

The legend separates ice-surface contours, ice-thickness isopachs, sub-ice bedrock contours and the aeromagnetic lineaments drawn south of 68°N. None supplies a river name. Historical mapping does not establish present ice margins, actual flow or hydraulic connectivity.

correspondence.finding: The regional PATP sheet preserves the western southeastward approach, the broad eastward corridor with its successive northward bends, and the later southeast descent. This distinctive sequence joins the route continued on the eastern sheet and is separate from the Churchill corridor to the north and the Romaine and Natashquan systems farther west or southwest. The regional scale supports drainage correspondence; it does not establish the exact source or a name for every initial feeder and lake passage.

The eastward continuation approaches and traverses the elongated Fourmont lake corridor before turning southeast. The eastern PATP hydrographic base shows the connecting channel and waterbody shapes. The provincial station profile directly names Little Mecatina River above Lac Fourmont, while the separate lake-outlet profile identifies Fourmont as a lake with an outlet into that river. The lake name is not treated as a river alias, and the model fragment join is not a naming boundary.

The short northeast branch approaches the main corridor near the Fourmont outlet and the southward turn. Its separate confluence and surrounding lake-channel setting are visible on the eastern PATP sheet. It remains a distinct tributary fragment; neither its whole local name nor a uniform Petit Mécatina name is inferred from model membership.

The long southern piece follows the eastern sheet’s channel from the northern lake passages through the extended southward descent, eastward bulge and renewed southern course. Rivière du Petit Mécatina is printed along this same lower corridor. The provincial hydrometric profile independently places the Petit Mécatina station upstream of the Nétagamiou junction. Neighboring Olomane and other coastal drainages remain separate.

At the coastal split, the selected line continues south rather than following the eastern branch. The forestry report’s original Figure 11 aerial mosaic separately labels the southward channel Rivière Nétagamiou and the eastward channel Rivière du Petit Mécatina. The federal salmon-river schedule independently describes Nétagamiou as extending upstream to Petit Mécatina and places its lower limit at the selected southern coastal outlet. Nétagamiou is therefore preserved as a distinct terminal name, not a synonym for the entire group or a tributary flowing toward Petit Mécatina.

The eastern end runs west through the upper drainage north of Horton Lake, with a southward dip before turning northwest. The ecological map shows this river corridor separately from the lake; the South Horton Plain description identifies the east-to-west watercourse as Horton River. The model endpoint is not certified as its named source.

The next long north-northwest reach traverses the dissected Horton Upland. The original map labels Horton River on this connected trunk and separates the dendritic feeder valleys from the Hornaday drainage farther east. Small tributary names are not distributed onto the selected line.

The central path bends northwest across the Horton plains, then makes its conspicuous westward elbow before resuming a northwest course. This sequence matches the mapped Horton trunk through the Central and West Horton settings; nearby lakes and the West River and Coal Creek tributaries retain separate scope.

The lower course turns north along the Smoking Hills, preserving the successive large meanders shown on the original hydrographic base. The report identifies Horton as crossing these hills in a confined valley, distinct from Anderson River on their western side.

The final coastal approach corresponds to the Horton–Franklin Bay setting. NASA imagery and direct text distinguish the active delta from abandoned meanders farther north. The model ends with a straight coastal extension, so that endpoint is not adopted as a surveyed modern mouth, current distributary or named abandoned channel.

scope_limit: MAIN_RIV groups and model mainstem roles do not establish a uniform name for every included reach, tributary or lake passage. Source observations support only the stated representative identity or hold.
publication_boundary: Own factual observations, attribution and official public URLs only; source originals, images, complete coordinates and private evidence remain omitted.
